subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Spite and Costly Punishment
description: Learn Spite and Costly Punishment in one minute.

hook.text: A player earns more than you. You can pay $1 to reduce their earnings by $3. You do it. Both are worse off.

buildup.text: Spiteful behavior reduces another's payoff at a cost to yourself. It's punishment without moral justification, only.

discovery.text: Experiments show people sometimes destroy value to close gaps. Status matters more than absolute wealth for some.

twist.text: Spite decreases with distance and anonymity. You are more spiteful toward those you can see and compare with directly.

climax.text: Recognizing spite in yourself is the first defense. Asking would I pay to hurt them if no one knew?

punchline.text: Spite costs you money to make someone else poorer.

quiz.question: When does spiteful behavior increase?
options: When people are anonymous and far apart
When people can see and directly compare with others
When absolute wealth is high for both parties

details.summary: Costly punishment occurs when individuals pay a personal cost to reduce another player's payoff, even with no direct benefit. Spite and punishment enforce social norms by making defection costly, sustaining cooperation in groups.
details.whyItMatters: The willingness to punish at personal cost is the enforcement mechanism behind social norms and cooperation. Without it, free riders would dominate, and cooperative institutions from workplace teams to public goods provision would collapse.
takeaways: People pay real costs to punish norm violators with no material benefit
Punishment sustains cooperation by making free-riding unprofitable
Punishment is stronger in cultures with strong cooperation norms

faq.question: Why would anyone pay to punish if it costs them?
faq.answer: Brain imaging shows punishment activates reward centers, suggesting it feels good. Evolutionarily, groups with punishers sustained cooperation better than those without. The personal cost is outweighed by the social benefit to the punisher's group.

faq.question: Can too much punishment be harmful?
faq.answer: Yes. Antisocial punishment, where cooperators are punished by defectors, exists in some cultures and undermines cooperation. Excessive punishment can also create fear-based compliance rather than intrinsic cooperation, which is less stable.
